question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 There’s an example where Matt did not establish the safe environment he was responsible for.

On a global platform modernization for a financial services client, Matt was the tech lead across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. Offshore teams were executing test cycles under delivery pressure. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, with existing documentation.

Matt relied on that documentation rather than verifying the controls. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. Communications went to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. But the non-punitive response he advocated did not extend to the client’s decision: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise” and that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

🐾 The distinction is what Matt owned, not simply whether he worked in consulting or in-house.

He grew the organization from **zero to 150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design. Across the centers, teams delivered **30+ product engagements** for **15+ Fortune 500 clients**. Reported results included **4X faster velocity**, zero-defect deployments, and **10-person teams** delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**. Delivery and client relationships contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business** by **FY23**. Clients also adopted the practices internally after engagements ended.

If the hiring concern is whether Matt has owned staffing, costs, engineering practices, and organizational continuity rather than only advised others, those were explicit parts of his job. The comparison with an in-house candidate would need that candidate’s record against the same responsibilities.

question: Has he worked in healthcare?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt actually did at the **Major U.S. Health System**.

The provider already had a condition management application, but care was reactive and clinicians had limited real-time patient insights. Matt led the initiative to add AI-powered capabilities, starting with diabetes management—not to replace the application. At the same time, the CIO raised concerns about processing sensitive medical information, HIPAA compliance, and patient privacy.

Matt designed and implemented the data lake, machine learning pipeline, LLM instance, and full-stack components to ingest and analyze data from electronic medical records, glucometers, activity trackers, and other devices. He integrated AI components into a mobile app, including a chat interface, medication reminders, lifestyle adjustments, and condition-specific guidance. He also established a feedback loop so patient data insights could refine the machine learning models over time.

For clinical teams, he provided training on interpreting AI-generated insights and incorporating them into treatment plans. Patients in the pilot could track health metrics, receive guidance, and monitor progress through the app.

On governance, Matt brought together legal, compliance, IT security, data science, and clinical representatives. He integrated anonymization, encryption, and differential privacy; created policies for data access, model transparency, and accountability; and established continuous monitoring and auditing. He regularly updated the CIO and executive team and adjusted the work based on feedback.

The team delivered a working MVP in **16 weeks**, using iterative product slicing and building an extensible foundation rather than a throwaway proof of concept. Clinical teams adopted the insights into treatment planning. The governance pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance, and executives approved consideration of broader AI implementation.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed, and what happened afterward.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying those controls, he assumed they were correct. He relied on inherited documentation without confirming its accuracy, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” and said leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

Following the incident, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach. His wording for the lesson: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”

answer_md:
🐾 Matt’s payments work spans payment-engine delivery, legacy-system consolidation, cross-border workflow design, and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional treasury systems had different data models, client configurations, and entitlement structures. The ACCESS Next Generation platform also needed payment capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries offering, with distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements for each payment type.

Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead, managing a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, alongside Message Authentication Code security and payment-type-specific permissions. For corporate users, he added contextual help explaining wire fields, tax payment codes, and FX parameters. He also delivered real-time reporting and single sign-on across treasury functions, so treasurers could work through a single portal rather than separate platforms.

He led the payments-workstream data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability without disruption to live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border and bulk payments. Matt designed end-to-end workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, including real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, and batch processing. The work delivered an implementation blueprint ready for development. Revised cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays, while training materials equipped business clients to manage multi-currency capabilities without ongoing support dependency.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox. Matt helped create cross-stack SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, and secure virtualized testing environments. His team validated the portal through a Client Onboarding Test Drive and used Lean Product and XP practices. Onboarding time fell, API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months**, and the team delivered over **261** additional story points beyond its commitment.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes payment-engine delivery, legacy-system consolidation, cross-border workflow design, and developer integration.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a **40+ person** blended team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. Matt helped create Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven API documentation, a secure sandbox, and virtualized testing environments. He delivered ACH, wire, and FX/cross-border modules, payment-integrity verification, and payment-type-specific permissions. Instead of retaining individual permission configuration, he introduced role-based profiles, bulk changes, and a centralized dashboard, reducing entitlement administration from days to minutes. He also led payments data migration with verification safeguards and compliance dashboards, without disrupting live payment operations.

The **Fiserv** program finished **3%** under budget, met **47/47** acceptance criteria, and launched with **zero critical defects**. Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the working model.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles with no visibility into work status. Requirements lived in **200-page** business requirements documents organized by system modules. Developers were in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland. Multiple deadlines had been missed, stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation, and PMO and compliance teams resisted moving to agile.

Matt replaced the single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture. He tracked the **47** acceptance criteria as Epics and decomposed requirements into persona-based user stories, rather than system modules. He established follow-the-sun synchronization: **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM CST** syncs for the reverse transition.

Instead of waiting until month **6** to discover branding, UI, and ADA compliance problems, Matt introduced bi-weekly sprint demos. When stakeholders lacked bandwidth for that feedback cadence, he negotiated dedicated review windows. He retained existing steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility.

For compliance, Matt used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments rather than static Word documents. He coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and incorporated JAWS/NVDA screen reader audits into the Definition of Done. Alongside that work, he introduced mandatory senior-developer code reviews, unit tests, and automated build quality gates.

The team moved to **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA gave **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones real-time visibility, and PMO and compliance accepted it for audit requirements. Across the program recovery, **Fiserv** received all **47** acceptance criteria with **zero critical defects at launch**, and the **\$8.5M** program finished **3% under budget**, saving **\$255K**.

🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **Norfolk Southern**.

Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform without stopping the railroad. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, while business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce. The client organization was accustomed to mainframe thinking, account leadership to waterfall delivery, and Matt’s team was learning a new working model as COVID forced remote work.

Matt brought business and technical contributors together for domain-driven design and event storming, mapping business functions, dependencies, and data flows. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB were built alongside it, with change data capture and reconciliation connecting the platforms. The architecture work also included the Boris Exercise, SNAP-E documentation, and anti-corruption layers for legacy integration.

When the client wanted more tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace through personas, prototypes, and weekly build-measure-learn iterations. He also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Domain experts paired with engineers through “I do, we do, you do,” spreading scarce legacy knowledge while client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native practices.

The work included a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership with the client and account leadership, audited the code and tests, rebuilt vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching. Daily rotating pairs, test cases before implementation, and testable stories reinforced the changes after those experts left.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive notifications. The quality-crisis failure mode did not recur, and client teams were co-creating in weekly iterations and gaining the skills to manage the new application themselves.
